newsitem.title: GERMANY: German brokers face tax payments after court move.
newsitem.headline: German brokers face tax payments after court move.

text.p: German stock brokers may face hefty back tax payments after a German court ended a long legal feud by ruling that a common bourse practice was permissible, German newspaper Die Welt reported at the weekend.

Frankfurt brokers who had participated in so-called dividend stripping in the late 1980s and 1990s now face paying up to 176 million marks in back taxes, Hans Noack, an official in the Hesse state finance ministry, told the newspaper.

The amount of back payments, which need to be made immediately, could be so high that they would force some brokers into bankruptcy, the paper said in a summary of an article to be published in the paper's Sunday edition.
Stripping a dividend meant that brokers would buy shares from investors shortly before a company paid its dividend and then sell the shares back to the original owner at a lower price.

In Germany companies generally pay a dividend and a tax credit to domestic investors. Foreign investors, who do not receive these tax credits, could however still benefit by selling the shares to domestic investors, like a broker. In addition to receiving the tax credit, these brokers or banks were also able to account for the difference between the higher purchase and lower resale prices as losses.
